{{short description|Geometric theorem regarding circles and triangles}}
[[File:Kosnita points.svg|300px|right|thumb|Kosnita point of an arbitrary triangle.
{{legend-line|solid black 2px|Triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid black 1px|Circumcircle (centered at circumcenter {{mvar|O}})}}
{{legend-line|solid #ff99ff 2px|[[Johnson circles]] (concur at {{mvar|O}})}}

In [[Euclidean geometry]], '''Kosnita's theorem''' is a property of certain [[circle]]s associated with an arbitrary [[triangle]].

Let {{math|△''ABC''}} be an arbitrary triangle, {{mvar|O}} its [[circumcenter]] and {{mvar|O{{sub|a}}}}, {{mvar|O{{sub|b}}}}, {{mvar|O{{sub|c}}}} are the circumcenters of three triangles {{math|△''OBC''}}, {{math|△''OCA''}}, and {{math|△''OAB''}} respectively.  The theorem asserts that the three [[straight line]]s {{mvar|AO{{sub|a}}}}, {{mvar|BO{{sub|b}}}}, and {{mvar|CO{{sub|c}}}} are concurrent.<ref name=wolframKosnita/> This result was established by the Romanian mathematician [[Cezar Coşniţă]] (1910–1962).<ref name=patrascu/>

Their point of concurrence is known as the triangle's '''Kosnita point''' (named by Rigby in 1997).  It is the [[isogonal conjugate]] of the [[nine-point center]].<ref name=grinberg2003/><ref name=rigby1997/> It is [[triangle center]] {{math|''X''(54)}} in [[Kimberling center|Clark Kimberling's list]].<ref name=kimberlingX54/>
